Drop with care: models registered with a training set depend on the features they were trained with. Deleting or changing a feature table can break batch scoring and serving for those models.

Upgrading a workspace feature table

A workspace feature table can be upgraded to a Unity Catalog feature table. Migrate the data into a Unity Catalog Delta table, define the primary key, and create the training and scoring code against the new table name. Move the consumers across before retiring the old table.

10. Paradigms and algorithm choice

Machine learning covers several paradigms, and the first decision in any project is which one matches the data and the question.

Types of machine learning

ParadigmDataGoalTypical model family
SupervisedInputs with known labelsPredict the label for unseen inputs. Models the conditional probability P(Y given X1 ... Xn)Regression and classification
UnsupervisedInputs with no labelsFind structure. Models the joint probability P(X1, X2, ..., Xn)Clustering, dimensionality reduction
Semi-supervisedA small labelled set plus many unlabelled rowsUse the few labels to infer labels for the larger setHybrid methods
Self-supervisedUnlabelled data, with labels made from the data itselfLearn patterns in a large dataset that transfer to another taskDeep networks, pretrained encoders
ReinforcementStates, actions and rewards from interactionLearn a policy that maximises cumulative rewardNeural networks and deep learning

Supervised tasks

  • Regression predicts a continuous output, such as sales, the number of viewers or a price.
  • Classification predicts a discrete category, such as yes or no, an image class or the presence of a disease.
  • Forecasting predicts future values from historical data, such as demand. The order of time matters, so it is a special case that needs time-aware splitting.

Unsupervised tasks

  • Clustering groups records with similar features. K-means is the common algorithm. It needs a number of clusters k and assigns each record to the nearest centroid.
  • Dimensionality reduction reduces the number of features while keeping most of the structure. Principal component analysis (PCA) is the standard method, and it projects data onto directions of greatest variance.
  • Embeddings turn items such as text, categories or images into dense vectors. Clustering the embeddings groups items by meaning rather than by raw column values.

Choosing a model family

ModelStrengthsWatch for
Linear regressionInterpretable coefficients, fast, a good baselineAssumes linear effects. Sensitive to scale and outliers
Logistic regressionProbabilistic output, interpretable, fastLinear decision boundary unless features are engineered
Decision treeCaptures nonlinearity and interactions. No scaling needed. Readable rulesOverfits deep trees. Unstable with small changes in data
Random forestStrong accuracy with little tuning. Averages many treesLess interpretable. Larger models
Gradient-boosted treesOften the best accuracy on tabular dataNeeds careful tuning to avoid overfitting
SVMEffective in high-dimensional spaces with clear marginsNeeds scaled features. Slow on very large data
K-nearest neighboursSimple and non-parametricSlow at prediction time. Needs scaled features
Neural networksLearn complex patterns, text, images, sequencesData hungry. Needs tuning and more compute
Rule of thumb: start with a simple baseline (a linear model or a shallow tree), then move to ensembles when the baseline is not good enough. Use the baseline to judge whether a complex model is worth its cost.

Estimators and transformers

Spark ML and scikit-learn both separate learning from transforming.

  • Transformer: an object with transform() that maps one DataFrame to another. A fitted model is a transformer, and so is a one-hot encoder.
  • Estimator: an object with fit() that learns from data and returns a fitted model. Logistic regression, a StringIndexer and an Imputer are estimators.
  • In scikit-learn, the same idea appears as fit and transform or predict methods on the same objects.
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression

indexer = StringIndexer(inputCol="city", outputCol="city_idx")   # Estimator
indexer_model = indexer.fit(train_df)                             # returns a Transformer
train_idx = indexer_model.transform(train_df)                     # Transformer

encoder = OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["city_idx"], outputCols=["city_vec"])  # Estimator
lr = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="features", labelCol="label")         # Estimator
Exam tip: an object that learns something from data, such as an imputer or a scaler, is an estimator until it is fitted. Its fitted version is the transformer. Calling transform on an unfitted estimator is an error.

Machine learning foundations to choose the algorithm

  • Classification or regression, decided by whether the target is categorical or continuous.
  • Labelled or unlabelled data, decided by whether a target column exists.
  • Data size and feature count, which affect training time and overfitting risk.
  • Interpretability requirements, which may force a linear model or a shallow tree.
  • Feature types, which decide encoding and scaling needs.

11. Pipelines, AutoML and imbalance

Building a model is a sequence of stages: prepare the data, split it, fit the preprocessing on training data, train, evaluate and iterate. Pipelines and AutoML make that sequence repeatable.

Training pipelines

A pipeline chains transformers and a final estimator, so one fit call trains every stage in order on the training data, and one transform or predict call runs the same steps on new data. It removes manual steps that differ between training and scoring, and it prevents leakage, because each stage is fitted on training rows only.

# scikit-learn
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)          # scaler learns the training mean and sd
pipe.predict(X_test)                # the same scaling is reused

# Spark ML
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline as SparkPipeline
spark_pipe = SparkPipeline(stages=[indexer, encoder, assembler, lr])
pipeline_model = spark_pipe.fit(train_df)     # returns a PipelineModel
predictions = pipeline_model.transform(test_df)
Spark naming: Pipeline is the estimator and PipelineModel is the fitted transformer returned by fit. Saving the PipelineModel stores every fitted step, so it can be reused for scoring later.

Machine learning runtime and environment

The ML runtime gives a consistent set of libraries for training. Use the same runtime for training and scoring, so package versions do not change results. The model's environment is recorded with it when it is logged, which supports reproducibility.

AutoML

AutoML takes a dataset and a target, then automatically profiles the data, applies preprocessing, selects features and algorithms, tunes hyperparameters and ranks the resulting models. For classification, regression and forecasting it produces leaderboards and generated notebooks with the code for each candidate.

AdvantageExplanation
SpeedA strong baseline in minutes rather than days
Best practice by defaultStandard splits, sensible preprocessing and tuning are applied consistently
TransparencyGenerated notebooks show exactly what was done, so the work can be audited and edited
TrackingEvery candidate is logged to MLflow with its parameters and metrics
Domain inputAnalysts can edit the generated code to add knowledge AutoML does not have

AutoML does not replace problem framing, metric choice or checks for leakage. Review the generated notebook and the metric before trusting the top model.

Data imbalance

When one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy by predicting the majority class every time. Methods that counter imbalance:

  • Cost-sensitive learning: assign a higher misclassification cost to the minority class during training. The model is penalised more for missing a rare case. In scikit-learn this is class_weight="balanced" or custom weights.
  • Oversampling the minority class, by duplicating rows or synthesising new ones (for example SMOTE). Apply it to training folds only.
  • Undersampling the majority class, which is fast but discards information.
  • Stratified splitting and stratified cross-validation, so every split keeps the class ratio.
  • Metric choice: use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or ROC-AUC rather than accuracy.
  • Threshold tuning: move the decision threshold on predicted probabilities to trade precision against recall.
Not a fix: collecting more data about the majority class, or normalising features, does not directly counter imbalance. Normalisation helps convergence and some models, but it does not change how the classes are weighted in the loss.

12. Metrics and the bias-variance trade-off

A metric turns a model's behaviour into a number that can be compared and optimised. Choosing the right metric is as important as choosing the model, because each metric rewards a different kind of success.

Regression metrics

MetricWhat it measuresRange and directionNotes
R-squared (R²)Proportion of the variance in the target explained by the modelUp to 1. Higher is better. Can be negative for a model worse than predicting the meanScale-free, but not a measure of error size
Mean absolute error (MAE)Average absolute difference between actual and predictedLower is better, in the target's unitsLess sensitive to outliers
Mean squared error (MSE)Average of squared differencesLower is better, in squared unitsPenalises large errors more heavily. Common for optimisation
Root mean squared error (RMSE)Square root of MSELower is better, in the target's unitsInterpretable like MAE, but still penalises large errors
 
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
mse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)
rmse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred) ** 0.5   # or root_mean_squared_error in recent scikit-learn
Version note: older code computes RMSE with mean_squared_error(..., squared=False). That argument is deprecated in newer scikit-learn, where root_mean_squared_error is provided instead. Both give the same result.

Classification metrics

Almost every classification metric starts from the confusion matrix. For a binary problem, with positive as the class of interest:

Predicted positivePredicted negative
Actual positiveTrue positive (TP)False negative (FN)
Actual negativeFalse positive (FP)True negative (TN)
MetricFormulaMeaning and when it matters
Accuracy(TP + TN) / totalProportion correct. Misleading with class imbalance
PrecisionTP / (TP + FP)Of the predicted positives, how many are right. Matters when false positives are costly, such as flagging legitimate email as spam
Recall (sensitivity)TP / (TP + FN)Of the actual positives, how many are found. Matters when false negatives are costly, such as missing a disease
F1 score2 times precision times recall / (precision + recall)Harmonic mean of precision and recall. A balance when both errors matter
Log loss (cross-entropy)Average of negative log of the probability given to the true classUses predicted probabilities. Penalises confident wrong predictions heavily. Lower is better
ROC-AUCArea under the curve of true positive rate against false positive rate, across all thresholdsMeasures how well the model ranks positives above negatives. 0.5 is random, 1 is perfect
 
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
                             f1_score, log_loss, roc_auc_score, confusion_matrix)

accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred)
recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred)
f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred)
cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)

# Probability-based metrics need scores, not hard labels
ll = log_loss(y_true, y_prob)
auc = roc_auc_score(y_true, y_prob)
Gotcha: roc_auc_score and log_loss need predicted probabilities or scores, not the 0 and 1 labels from predict. Passing hard labels gives a misleading AUC and a meaningless log loss.

Clustering metrics

  • Silhouette score compares, for each point, the distance to its own cluster with the distance to the nearest other cluster. Values near 1 mean well-separated clusters, values near 0 mean overlap. It is computed with silhouette_score(X, labels).
  • Elbow method plots the within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) against the number of clusters k. Choose the k where adding clusters stops giving a large improvement, the elbow.
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

labels = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=42, n_init=10).fit_predict(X)
score = silhouette_score(X, labels)

inertias = [KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10).fit(X).inertia_
            for k in range(1, 7)]

Metrics on transformed targets

If the target or a feature was log-transformed, exponentiate the predictions before scoring, as covered in the Data Preparation realm. Metrics computed on the log scale answer a different question.

Bias, variance and model complexity

  • Bias is error from overly simple assumptions. A high-bias model underfits: it is wrong on training data and on new data.
  • Variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample. A high-variance model overfits: it does well on training data and worse on new data.
  • Increasing complexity (deeper trees, more features, more neurons) lowers bias and raises variance. Reducing complexity does the opposite.
  • The goal is the complexity at which total error on unseen data is lowest. Regularisation, pruning, more data and early stopping move the balance toward lower variance.
SymptomTraining scoreValidation scoreLikely cause and fix
UnderfittingLowLow, close to trainingToo simple. Add features or capacity, reduce regularisation
OverfittingHighMuch lowerToo complex or too little data. Regularise, simplify, add data, use cross-validation
Good fitHighSimilar and highBalanced complexity

13. Hyperparameters and search methods

A model has two kinds of numbers. Parameters are learned from the data, such as regression coefficients or tree split thresholds. Hyperparameters are set before training and control how learning happens. Hyperparameter tuning, also called model tuning, searches for the hyperparameter values that give the best performance on validation data.

Common hyperparameters

  • Random forest: maximum depth of the trees, number of trees, number of features considered at each split.
  • Linear models: regularisation strength, and whether to normalise features.
  • Gradient boosting: learning rate, number of boosting rounds, tree depth.
  • SVM: the penalty C, the kernel, and the kernel width gamma.
  • Neural networks: the activation function, the number of neurons in each hidden layer, learning rate.
Parameter or hyperparameter? If training sets it from the data, it is a parameter. If you choose it before training begins, it is a hyperparameter. The number of trees is a hyperparameter; the split at a tree node is a parameter.

Search methods

MethodHow it worksStrengthsWeaknesses
Grid searchDefines a grid of values and tries every combinationSystematic. Finds the best combination within the gridCost grows multiplicatively with each hyperparameter
Random searchSamples combinations from distributionsMore efficient in high dimensions. Often finds good values fasterNo guarantee of the best combination, and it does not cover the grid
Bayesian optimisationBuilds a probability model of the objective and uses past results to pick promising values nextUses fewer trials on expensive models. Often the most efficientMore complex to implement. Overhead on very cheap models

Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) is a popular Bayesian method. It models the good and the bad trials separately and proposes values that are likely to be in the good region. It is the default sampler in Optuna and is the algorithm behind Hyperopt's tpe.suggest.

Cross-validation as the scoring step

Tuning uses validation data, and a single validation split can be noisy. Cross-validation scores each combination over k folds and averages the results, so the choice is less sensitive to one lucky split.

Train-validation splitK-fold cross-validation
One fit per combinationk fits per combination
Cheapk times the compute
Estimate can be noisy with small dataAverage over folds is more stable
Uses a fixed portion of the data for validationEvery row is used for validation once
Counting the models in a grid search. Multiply the number of values for each hyperparameter to get the number of combinations, then multiply by the number of folds. Example: three values of C, two kernels and three values of gamma give 3 times 2 times 3 = 18 combinations. With 5-fold cross-validation, 18 times 5 = 90 models are trained. The optional final refit on the full training data adds one more fit, but the standard count is 90.
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.svm import SVC

param_grid = {
    "C": [0.1, 1, 10],
    "kernel": ["linear", "rbf"],
    "gamma": [0.01, 0.1, 1]
}
search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), param_grid, cv=5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(search.best_params_, search.best_score_)
Grid search with a kernel that ignores gamma: a linear kernel does not use gamma, so some grid combinations are redundant. The count rule still applies, because the grid is still evaluated.

Parallelising tuning

  • Single-node models can be tuned in parallel with n_jobs=-1 in scikit-learn search classes, which uses all available cores.
  • Trials of a single search are independent, so they parallelise well. Each trial is a separate model fit.
  • Spark-based parallelism distributes trials across the cluster. Hyperopt's SparkTrials does this, and Optuna can run trials across processes.
  • Parallel trials cannot learn from each other within the same round, so Bayesian methods trade a little efficiency for parallel speed.

Hyperopt and fmin

Hyperopt is a Bayesian optimisation library that provides the fmin function. You define an objective function that returns a loss to minimise, a search space, an algorithm and a budget of evaluations.

from hyperopt import fmin, tpe, hp, Trials, STATUS_OK
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

space = {
    "max_depth": hp.quniform("max_depth", 2, 12, 1),
    "n_estimators": hp.quniform("n_estimators", 50, 300, 10),
}

def objective(params):
    model = RandomForestRegressor(
        max_depth=int(params["max_depth"]),
        n_estimators=int(params["n_estimators"]),
        random_state=42)
    rmse = -cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=3,
                            scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean()
    return {"loss": rmse, "status": STATUS_OK}

trials = Trials()
best = fmin(fn=objective, space=space, algo=tpe.suggest,
            max_evals=50, trials=trials)
Exam tip: quniform returns floats, so cast integer hyperparameters with int() inside the objective. fmin minimises, so return a loss that goes down as the model improves. To maximise a score, return its negative.
Deprecation note: Hyperopt is scheduled for removal from the ML runtime with DBR ML 17.0 and later. Code written for it needs migrating, for example to Optuna, before the runtime is upgraded.

Ray Tune

Ray Tune is another scalable tuning library. It offers grid and advanced search algorithms and runs trials across a cluster. It is a good choice when tuning must scale beyond one machine.

14. Tuning with Optuna

Optuna is an open-source hyperparameter optimisation framework. It automates the search, adapts it using earlier results, and records every trial. It is written in Python with few dependencies, and it works with any framework, including scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch, TensorFlow and Keras, because it only needs an objective function that returns a number.

Terminology

TermMeaning
Objective functionA Python function that takes a trial, builds a model with the suggested values, and returns the metric to optimise
TrialOne call of the objective function, with one set of suggested values
StudyAn optimisation session: a collection of trials and the settings used to choose the next ones
Parameter (in Optuna)A variable being optimised, usually the loss or the accuracy
Search spaceThe ranges and choices suggested for each parameter, defined inside the objective
SamplerThe strategy that proposes the next values. The default is TPE
PrunerStops unpromising trials early, using intermediate results. Beyond the core exam scope

Defining the search space

Inside the objective, trial suggests values. Each suggest call names a parameter and gives its range or choices:

MethodSuggests
trial.suggest_int(name, low, high)Integers in a range
trial.suggest_float(name, low, high)Floats in a range. Use log=True for values spread over orders of magnitude, and step= for a grid of floats
trial.suggest_categorical(name, choices)One value from a list
trial.suggest_uniform and trial.suggest_discrete_uniformOlder names. Deprecated in favour of suggest_float with the matching options

A complete study

import optuna
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

def objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 50, 300),
        "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 2, 16),
        "max_features": trial.suggest_categorical("max_features", ["sqrt", "log2"]),
        "min_samples_leaf": trial.suggest_int("min_samples_leaf", 1, 10),
    }
    model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42, **params)
    score = cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=3, scoring="f1").mean()
    return score

study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize")
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50, n_jobs=-1)

print(study.best_params)     # dictionary of the best values
print(study.best_value)      # the best objective value
print(study.best_trial)      # the full best trial
Direction matters: direction="maximize" is used for scores such as accuracy or F1. Use "minimize" for losses such as RMSE. Choosing the wrong direction makes the study find the worst model.

Reading the results

  • study.best_params, a dictionary of the best parameter values.
  • study.best_value, the objective value of the best trial.
  • study.best_trial, the best trial object, including its parameters and value.
  • study.best_trials, the set of Pareto-optimal trials, used for multi-objective studies. For a single objective it is not the usual choice.
  • study.trials_dataframe(), a pandas table of every trial, useful for plotting progress.

How Optuna chooses the next trial

The sampler looks at finished trials, models which regions gave good values, and proposes new values from the promising regions. The default TPE sampler does this with a Bayesian model. Grid and random samplers are also available, and the sampler choice does not change the objective or the search space.

Tracking trials with MLflow

Optuna's MLflowCallback logs each trial's parameters and metrics to MLflow automatically. Each trial becomes a child run of a parent run, so all the trials of one study stay grouped together in the experiment.

from optuna.integration.mlflow import MLflowCallback

mlflow_callback = MLflowCallback(
    tracking_uri="databricks",
    create_experiment=False,
    mlflow_kwargs={
        "experiment_id": experiment_id,
        "nested": True
    }
)

study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50, callbacks=[mlflow_callback])
  • tracking_uri="databricks" sends the runs to the Databricks workspace's MLflow.
  • create_experiment=False uses the experiment you name, rather than creating a new one.
  • nested: True groups the trial runs under a parent run.
  • Callbacks run after each trial, so logging happens as the study progresses.
Parallel trials and MLflow: logging from parallel workers is easy to misconfigure. After a study that uses n_jobs greater than 1, check in the MLflow UI that every trial sits under the expected parent run.

Retrieving the best model

The study records the best parameters, but the model itself must be refitted with those parameters on the full training data and then logged or registered. Pulling the best run from MLflow is an alternative when the trials logged their models: query the experiment for the best run by its metric and load that run's model.

import mlflow

best_run = mlflow.search_runs(
    experiment_ids=[experiment_id],
    order_by=["metrics.f1 DESC"],
    max_results=1
).iloc[0]

best_model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(f"runs:/{best_run.run_id}/model")
Exam tip: a study is the optimisation session and a trial is one call of the objective. Questions about "how many trials" count objective calls, while questions about "how many models" in a grid search count fits, which are trials multiplied by folds.

15. Serving modes: batch, streaming, real-time and edge

Model deployment is the step that moves a trained model out of the development notebook and into a production environment, where end users or other systems can receive predictions or insights. A model creates value only once something calls it: a scheduled job, a stream of events, or an application making requests. The right deployment method depends on how quickly a prediction is needed, how many records must be scored, and how often the input data changes.

The full machine learning lifecycle runs from a business problem and success criteria, through data collection, preprocessing and feature engineering, and model training and evaluation on static historical data. Deployment and production is where the model meets continuously changing data. Monitoring then tells you when performance drifts, which triggers retraining and redeployment.

Four deployment methods

MethodThroughputLatencyTypical example
BatchHighHigh (hours to days)Periodic customer churn scores
Streaming (pipeline)ModerateModerate (seconds to minutes)Scoring a continuous feed of listening or click events
Real-time (request and response)Lower per endpointLow (milliseconds)Fraud check during a payment, chatbot reply
Edge or embeddedLimited by the deviceLow, on deviceSensor on a farm reading humidity and classifying locally

Batch deployment

Batch inference generates predictions on a regular schedule. A job reads the new records, scores them with the model, and writes the results to persistent storage, where downstream consumers such as BI dashboards pick them up. It is the most common deployment strategy.

  • Use it when immediate predictions are not necessary, predictions can be made in bulk, the number of new records is large, and the input changes or arrives at intervals of roughly 30 minutes or more.
  • Advantages: the cheapest method, easy to implement, efficient per record, and able to handle very high volume.
  • Limitations: high latency, predictions go stale between runs, and it is a poor fit for rapidly changing data or streaming requirements.

Streaming (pipeline) deployment

Streaming deployment scores records continuously as they arrive rather than waiting for a batch window. A pipeline reads an incoming stream, applies the model in its final step, and writes predictions to a table, so downstream systems see results within seconds to minutes. It is event driven, so systems can act sooner than with batch.

  • Advantages: lower latency than batch, and predictions arrive while they can still be acted on.
  • Limitations: costlier than batch, more complicated to develop, maintain and monitor, lower throughput than batch on the same hardware, and resource intensive because compute has to keep running to process the feed.

Real-time deployment

Real-time deployment produces a prediction in response to each request, usually through a REST API. Typical uses are fraud detection during a transaction, a chatbot answering a user, or a recommendation displayed while a page loads. Requirements usually include low latency, immediate action, 24/7 availability and continuous monitoring. Large language models are increasingly served this way.

Building real-time serving yourself means fast, scalable serving infrastructure that is costly to build and maintain, plus tooling for packaging, scaling, security and monitoring. Model Serving on Databricks is the managed option covered in the last chapter of this realm.

Edge and embedded deployment

Edge deployment runs inference on local hardware such as a phone, gateway or sensor. Choose it when connectivity is offline or unreliable, when latency must be very low, or when data has to stay on the device for security or compliance. The model is exported to a portable runtime such as ONNX Runtime or TensorFlow Lite, as described in the next chapter.

Exam tip: match the mode to the latency and arrival pattern. Results read tomorrow morning means batch. Results needed within seconds on a continuous feed means streaming. A caller waiting on a web request means real-time.
Common confusion: streaming and real-time are different. A streaming pipeline moves records from one table to another as they arrive. A real-time endpoint answers individual REST requests.

16. Packaging models with MLflow for deployment

Before a model can be deployed anywhere, it has to be packaged so that any target can load it. MLflow provides that packaging through the MLflow Model format and the Model Registry. MLflow has four components: Tracking records experiments (code, data, configuration and results), Projects packages code for reproducible runs, Models defines a general model format that supports many deployment tools, and the Model Registry manages the model lifecycle centrally.

Packaging with MLflow keeps the deployment environment consistent with the training environment, because the dependencies and configuration travel with the model. The same packaged model can be served by a local server, in containers on Kubernetes or a cloud service, or by Databricks Model Serving.

Anatomy of an MLflow Model

An MLflow Model is a directory that holds arbitrary files plus an MLmodel file. The MLmodel file lists the flavors the model can be viewed in and can also carry metadata such as a signature and an input example. Saving a scikit-learn model with mlflow.sklearn.save_model(model, "my_model") writes a directory like this:

my_model/
├── MLmodel
├── model.pkl
├── conda.yaml
├── python_env.yaml
└── requirements.txt

A trimmed MLmodel file looks like this:

sklearn:
  sklearn_version: 0.19.1
  pickled_model: model.pkl
python_function:
  loader_module: mlflow.sklearn

Flavors and the python_function interface

A flavor is one way of viewing the same saved model. The python_function flavor, exposed as mlflow.pyfunc, is the generic interface. A deployment tool that knows only pyfunc can load any MLflow Python model and call predict, which is why pyfunc is the default route for batch jobs, Spark and serving. The pyfunc API includes log_model, save_model, load_model and predict.

Built-in flavors cover scikit-learn, Spark MLlib, PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX, Hugging Face models and LLM libraries such as LangChain and OpenAI. You can also define custom flavors.

Signatures and input examples

A signature records the input and output schema of a model. An input example is a sample payload. Both are stored in the MLmodel file, and they let pyfunc and serving check that incoming columns and types match what the model expects.

from mlflow.models import infer_signature

signature = infer_signature(X_train, model.predict(X_train))
mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
    model, "model", signature=signature, input_example=X_train.head(3)
)

Registering in Unity Catalog and loading by alias

import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")
mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri=f"runs:/{run_id}/model",   # run_id comes from the training run
    name="catalog.schema.churn_model",   # three-level name required in Unity Catalog
)

client = MlflowClient()
client.set_registered_model_alias(
    name="catalog.schema.churn_model", alias="champion", version=3
)

model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/catalog.schema.churn_model@champion")

The Unity Catalog registry stores models with three-level names and gives centralized governance, permissions, lineage, versioning, tags and annotations. Aliases such as champion and challenger mark which version is in use. Code that loads by alias picks up a promoted version the next time it runs, without a code change. A serving endpoint is different: each served version is pinned, so promoting a new champion means updating the endpoint configuration.

Custom models with PythonModel

When a model needs logic beyond a single estimator, such as preprocessing, a business rule or several artifacts, wrap it in a subclass of mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel. load_context runs once when the model is loaded and can read the artifacts logged with it. predict runs on each request or batch of rows.

import joblib
import mlflow.pyfunc

class ChurnWrapper(mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel):
    def load_context(self, context):
        # base_model.pkl was written with joblib.dump before logging
        self.model = joblib.load(context.artifacts["base_model"])

    def predict(self, context, model_input, params=None):
        proba = self.model.predict_proba(model_input)[:, 1]
        return (proba >= 0.5).astype(int)

with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        artifact_path="model",   # MLflow 3 uses name= in place of artifact_path
        python_model=ChurnWrapper(),
        artifacts={"base_model": "base_model.pkl"},
        signature=signature,
    )

The wrapper class must be importable wherever the model is loaded, so keep it in a Python file or in the logging notebook, and make sure its dependencies are captured in the logged environment.

Exporting for edge runtimes

When the target cannot run the Python environment, such as a phone, a gateway or specialized hardware, export the model to ONNX and score it with ONNX Runtime. The ONNX file is logged as its own flavor, and the consumer reads it without MLflow.

import numpy as np
import mlflow
import onnxmltools
import onnxruntime

onnx_model = onnxmltools.convert_keras(keras_model)
mlflow.onnx.log_model(onnx_model, "onnx_model")

session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(onnx_model.SerializeToString())
input_name = session.get_inputs()[0].name
predictions = session.run(None, {input_name: data_np.astype(np.float32)})[0]

17. Batch and streaming inference in pipelines

Batch and pipeline inference run on Spark, Delta tables and Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines. Choosing the right tool depends on whether the data fits on one machine, whether features come from a feature table, and whether the scoring must run continuously.

Batch inference with pandas

Pandas batch inference loads the model on the driver with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model and calls predict on a pandas DataFrame. It suits data that fits comfortably in driver memory, such as a few hundred megabytes. Write the results back to Delta with Spark.

import mlflow.pyfunc

model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/catalog.schema.churn_model@champion")
feature_cols = ["tenure", "monthly_charges", "support_calls"]

features_pdf = spark.table("catalog.schema.customer_features").toPandas()
features_pdf["churn_score"] = model.predict(features_pdf[feature_cols])

spark.createDataFrame(features_pdf).write.mode("overwrite") \
    .saveAsTable("catalog.schema.churn_predictions")
Watch out: toPandas() collects every row to the driver. For data larger than driver memory, use a Spark UDF so the scoring is distributed.

Distributed batch inference with a Spark UDF

mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf turns a pyfunc model into a Spark UDF. The model is loaded on the executors and each executor scores its share of the rows, usually in vectorized batches passed as pandas Series. Pass the feature columns in the order the model signature expects, and set result_type to match the model output.

import mlflow.pyfunc
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

predict_udf = mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(
    spark,
    model_uri="models:/catalog.schema.churn_model@champion",
    result_type="double",
)

feature_cols = ["tenure", "monthly_charges", "support_calls"]
scored = (
    spark.table("catalog.schema.customer_features")
    .withColumn("churn_score", predict_udf(*[col(c) for c in feature_cols]))
)
scored.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("catalog.schema.churn_predictions")

Batch scoring with Feature Store

If the model was trained with features from an offline feature table, the batch job only needs the primary keys. score_batch joins the features from the feature table, applies the model and returns the predictions. The model must have been logged with fe.log_model, which stores the feature lookup metadata with it. The legacy Feature Store client exposes the same method as FeatureStoreClient.score_batch.

from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient

fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()
new_customers = spark.table("catalog.schema.customers_to_score").select("customer_id")

predictions = fe.score_batch(
    model_uri="models:/catalog.schema.churn_model@champion",
    df=new_customers,
)
predictions.write.mode("append").saveAsTable("catalog.schema.churn_predictions")

An offline feature table is a Delta table with a primary key. It suits batch inference and training, but it is not optimized for real-time latency.

Delta layout and maintenance for batch tables

  • Liquid clustering replaces table partitioning and ZORDER. Enable it with CLUSTER BY (Databricks Runtime 13.3 or later). Databricks recommends it for all new Delta tables, and it manages the layout for you.
  • OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into larger ones, which speeds up reads. On tables that do not use liquid clustering, OPTIMIZE table ZORDER BY (col) also co-locates related values.
  • Predictive optimization finds tables that would benefit from maintenance and runs OPTIMIZE and VACUUM for you. Enable it at the account level first, then per catalog or schema.
  • VACUUM deletes data files that the table no longer references, once they are older than the retention period (7 days by default).
CREATE TABLE catalog.schema.customer_features (customer_id BIGINT, tenure INT)
USING DELTA
CLUSTER BY (customer_id);

ALTER CATALOG catalog1 ENABLE PREDICTIVE OPTIMIZATION;

Streaming inference with Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines

Delta Live Tables (DLT) is now branded Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, and the older name, Delta Live Tables, is still common in documentation and existing code. You declare tables in SQL or Python, and the pipeline works out the dependency graph, runs updates in order, retries failures, scales compute and enforces data quality. Two kinds of table are common. A streaming table processes new rows incrementally and is the usual target for ingestion and scoring. A materialized view stores the result of a query and refreshes it. Older DLT syntax used CREATE LIVE TABLE and CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE.

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events
AS SELECT *
FROM cloud_files("/Volumes/catalog/schema/raw_events", "json");

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW clean_events
AS SELECT user_id, event_type, event_ts
FROM bronze_events;

Auto Loader, exposed in pipelines through cloud_files, picks up new files as they land in cloud storage and processes each one once. It can infer the schema, accept schema hints, and evolve the schema automatically. It reads JSON, CSV, Avro and Parquet.

The inference step is the last table in the pipeline. The model is applied as a Spark UDF, so each executor scores its rows and pipeline autoscaling sizes the compute:

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
import mlflow.pyfunc

predict_udf = mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(
    spark, "models:/catalog.schema.churn_model@champion", result_type="double"
)

@dp.table(name="scored_events")
def scored_events():
    return (
        spark.readStream.table("clean_events")
        .withColumn("score", predict_udf(col("feature_a"), col("feature_b")))
    )

Data quality in the pipeline

Expectations state a rule that every row should satisfy. The ON VIOLATION clause sets the action. DROP ROW removes the failing rows, FAIL UPDATE stops the update, and with no clause the violation is recorded in the pipeline metrics and the row is kept. All of these are tracked in pipeline metrics and the event log, which also provide a lineage diagram and row-level logging. Notifications can be sent with Databricks SQL alerts.

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE clean_events (
  CONSTRAINT valid_user EXPECT (user_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,
  CONSTRAINT valid_ts EXPECT (event_ts IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
)
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM bronze_events;
Exam tip: a Spark UDF inside a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline is the usual answer when a streaming inference job needs elastic compute and no network call per row. Calling a serving endpoint from a UDF adds latency, cost and rate limits, so use it only when the model cannot run in Spark.

18. Real-time inference with Model Serving

Real-time deployment returns a prediction immediately in response to a request. Databricks Model Serving hosts models behind REST endpoints, so applications can call them without managing servers. Model Serving covers three kinds of served content: custom models (your MLflow models), Foundation Model APIs (curated foundation models behind simple APIs), and external models (third-party model APIs governed through the same layer).

What a serving endpoint provides

  • Deploys any MLflow model from Unity Catalog as a REST API on serverless compute.
  • CPU and GPU support, with GPUs for deploying large language models.
  • Autoscaling within a selected workload size range, with compute kept warm for fast scale-up.
  • Scale to zero for predictable traffic that is not 24/7, which saves cost at the price of a cold start after idle periods.
  • Low overhead latency and high throughput are the stated goals, and availability is published as 99.5%. Check current documentation for the exact figures.
  • Security through PrivateLink and IP allowlists, and governance through Unity Catalog.
  • Monitoring through a ready-made metrics dashboard, an export API for external observability platforms, and alerts through Databricks SQL.
  • Integration with Feature Store lookups and Vector Search, so the endpoint can fetch features or vectors itself.

Endpoint-centric workflow

Each endpoint has a stable scoring URI, so callers never change when the models behind it change. One endpoint can host several models, and the same model can sit behind several endpoints. Each deployed model version is a served entity with its own workload size, scale-to-zero setting and traffic share. Staged rollout and A/B testing both come from changing those shares.

Deploying a custom model

The steps are: log the model and register a version in Unity Catalog, create the endpoint with that version, and then query it. You can create the endpoint in the Serving UI, or through the REST API, the Python SDK, the Go SDK, Terraform, or a Lakeflow Job that automates the deployment in a CI/CD process.

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from databricks.sdk.service.serving import EndpointCoreConfigInput, ServedEntityInput

w = WorkspaceClient()
w.serving_endpoints.create_and_wait(
    name="churn-endpoint",
    config=EndpointCoreConfigInput(
        served_entities=[
            ServedEntityInput(
                entity_name="catalog.schema.churn_model",
                entity_version="3",
                workload_size="Small",
                scale_to_zero_enabled=True,
            )
        ]
    ),
)

The REST equivalent is a POST to /api/2.0/serving-endpoints with the same configuration in the body.

Querying the endpoint

Requests go to the endpoint's invocations route. The body holds the rows as dataframe_records, a list of objects, or as dataframe_split, with separate columns and data arrays. The response contains a predictions list.

curl -X POST "https://<workspace-url>/serving-endpoints/churn-endpoint/invocations" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"dataframe_records": [{"tenure": 12, "monthly_charges": 70.5, "support_calls": 2}]}'
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

w = WorkspaceClient()
response = w.serving_endpoints.query(
    name="churn-endpoint",
    dataframe_records=[{"tenure": 12, "monthly_charges": 70.5, "support_calls": 2}],
)
print(response.predictions)
Watch out: scale to zero means the first request after an idle period waits for the endpoint to start. Do not use it where the latency target cannot absorb a cold start.

Splitting traffic between versions

Traffic splitting sends a share of requests to each served entity behind one endpoint. Use it for a canary release, staged rollout or A/B test. The percentages must add up to 100, and every route names a served entity. The configuration below is updated with a PUT to /api/2.0/serving-endpoints/{name}/config.

{
  "served_entities": [
    {"name": "churn-v3", "entity_name": "catalog.schema.churn_model",
     "entity_version": "3", "workload_size": "Small", "scale_to_zero_enabled": true},
    {"name": "churn-v4", "entity_name": "catalog.schema.churn_model",
     "entity_version": "4", "workload_size": "Small", "scale_to_zero_enabled": true}
  ],
  "traffic_config": {
    "routes": [
      {"served_entity_name": "churn-v3", "traffic_percentage": 90},
      {"served_entity_name": "churn-v4", "traffic_percentage": 10}
    ]
  }
}

Splitting inside one endpoint keeps a single stable URI for callers. If you need traffic divided between separate endpoints, the calling application does the routing. Once the new version proves itself, move its share to 100 percent and remove the old served entity.

Real-time inference with online features

Online feature serving removes feature logic from the caller. Features are stored in an offline feature table (a Delta table with a primary key), registered as lookups when the model is logged, and synced to an online table. At inference time the endpoint fetches the features automatically, so the request carries only the key.

from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient, FeatureLookup

fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()
training_set = fe.create_training_set(
    df=labels_df,  # columns: customer_id, churned
    feature_lookups=[
        FeatureLookup(table_name="catalog.schema.customer_features",
                      lookup_key="customer_id")
    ],
    label="churned",
)
fe.log_model(
    model=model,
    artifact_path="model",
    flavor=mlflow.sklearn,
    training_set=training_set,
    registered_model_name="catalog.schema.churn_model",
)

A request for this model needs only the key: {"dataframe_records": [{"customer_id": 1042}]}.

Feature functions compute on-demand features at inference time. They are Python UDFs governed by Unity Catalog, and they take inputs from the request and bindings defined during training. They support every type that Feature Store supports except MapType and ArrayType. Online feature stores offer low latency and high throughput, serverless autoscaling, point-in-time correctness for training data, and scheduled updates.

Exam tip: a single endpoint can split traffic between served versions, and scale to zero reduces idle cost. Automatic feature lookups need a model logged with feature metadata and an online table that is kept in sync.

19. MLflow Tracking Fundamentals

MLflow is an open-source platform for the machine learning lifecycle. It is co-developed by Databricks and the wider community and is pre-installed on Databricks Runtime for ML. It has four components: Tracking, which records and compares experiments; Evaluation, which automates metric computation for common supervised tasks; Models, a unified packaging format that works across frameworks; and the Model Registry, which provides version control and managed deployment. MLflow can be used from Python, R, Java, the command line and the REST API.

Experiments

An experiment is the top-level container for a set of related runs. Teams create one to explore different configurations, parameters or algorithms for the same problem. There are two kinds:

  • Notebook experiment: tied to the notebook that creates the runs. It is created automatically when training runs in a notebook that has no experiment set.
  • Workspace experiment: stored at a path you choose, such as /Users/name@example.com/churn. Several notebooks can write runs into the same workspace experiment.
import mlflow
mlflow.set_experiment("/Users/name@example.com/churn")

Runs

A run is one execution of data science code. Each run belongs to exactly one experiment, and a run can be nested under a parent run. The table lists what a run holds.

ElementWhat it holdsTypical logging call
ParametersKey-value inputs such as hyperparameters, stored as stringslog_param, log_params
MetricsNumeric results, optionally with a step number to build a historylog_metric, log_metrics
TagsMutable key-value labelsset_tag, set_tags
ArtifactsAny files or folders: plots, data samples, JSON, textlog_artifact, log_artifacts, log_figure, log_text, log_dict
ModelModel folder with MLmodel, conda.yaml or requirements, and the serialized modelmlflow.sklearn.log_model and other flavors
MetadataRun ID, experiment ID, status, start and end times, user and sourceRecorded automatically

Manual logging inside a run looks like this. Used as a context manager, the run ends automatically when the block exits, even if an error is raised.

import mlflow
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="rf-baseline") as run:
    mlflow.log_params({"n_estimators": 200, "max_depth": 8})
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=8)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    preds = model.predict(X_test)

    mlflow.log_metric("f1", f1_score(y_test, preds))
    mlflow.log_dict({"features": list(X_train.columns)}, "features.json")
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="random_forest_model")
    run_id = run.info.run_id

Nested runs group child runs, for example one child per hyperparameter setting, under a parent run:

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="depth-search") as parent:
    for depth in [4, 8, 16]:
        with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"depth-{depth}", nested=True):
            mlflow.log_param("max_depth", depth)
Gotchas. Parameters are strings and can be logged once per key within a run. Logging a different value for an existing key raises an error, so log parameters before training or start a new run. Metrics, by contrast, can be logged repeatedly. Log a step with each value to build a history that the UI plots as a curve, for example mlflow.log_metric("train_loss", loss, step=epoch).

Artifacts

Artifacts are stored under the run and can be downloaded later. log_artifact copies one local file, log_artifacts copies a whole folder, log_figure saves a plot figure, log_text saves a string, and log_dict saves a dictionary as JSON. The logged model is also an artifact, stored with its MLmodel descriptor and environment files.

Autologging and custom logging

Autologging records parameters, metrics, the trained model and related details for supported libraries without extra code. Call mlflow.autolog() to enable it for every supported library, or a framework-specific form such as mlflow.sklearn.autolog(). Databricks Autologging is enabled by default in notebooks on Databricks Runtime for ML and can be turned off with mlflow.autolog(disable=True).

Custom logging covers what autologging cannot know: a business-specific score, a decision threshold, a plot, or a configuration file. Custom calls can be added inside the same active run as autologging.

mlflow.autolog()
with mlflow.start_run():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    mlflow.log_metric("super_score", custom_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)))

The MLflow Client API

MlflowClient gives programmatic access to experiments and runs, which is how selection and promotion decisions are automated. Common methods include search_experiments, get_experiment_by_name, search_runs, get_run, get_metric_history and list_artifacts.

search_runs takes experiment_ids (a list), filter_string (a SQL-like condition), order_by (a list such as ["metrics.rmse ASC"]) and max_results. Filters refer to metrics., params., tags. and attributes. keys. Parameter and tag values must be quoted strings, while metric values are compared as numbers.

from mlflow import MlflowClient

client = MlflowClient()
runs = client.search_runs(
    experiment_ids=["1234"],
    filter_string="params.model = 'random_forest' AND metrics.rmse < 10",
    order_by=["metrics.rmse ASC"],
    max_results=5,
)
if runs:
    best = runs[0]
    print(best.info.run_id, best.data.metrics["rmse"])

Identifying the best run

Choose the sort direction from what the metric means. Accuracy, F1, R-squared and ROC AUC are better when larger, so sort DESC. RMSE, MAE, MSE and log loss are better when smaller, so sort ASC. Always check that the result list is not empty before indexing it.

What the MLflow UI shows

The experiment page lists its runs in a table. Columns include run name, creation time, duration, user, source, and each logged parameter and metric. You can filter and search runs, select several to compare side by side, and plot metrics. Opening a run shows its overview (run ID, status, start and end times, duration, user and source notebook), its parameters, metrics with their history, tags, the artifact tree including the logged model and its signature, and a control to register the model. The UI suits exploration; the Client API suits automation.

Exam tip. When a question asks for the best run programmatically, look for search_runs with a filter_string, an order_by on the correct metric direction, and max_results. The UI answers the same question visually but cannot be scripted.

20. Unity Catalog Model Registry

The Unity Catalog model registry stores registered models in the same three-level namespace used for tables: catalog.schema.model. Because models live in Unity Catalog, they are governed by its privileges, can be shared across every workspace attached to the same metastore, and link back to the data used to train them.

Core objects

ObjectMeaningExample
Registered modelNamed container for all versions of one modelml_prod.churn.churn_classifier
Model versionInteger-numbered snapshot created by each registration. Its artifacts cannot be changed afterwardsVersion 4
AliasMovable named pointer to one version of a registered modelchampion, challenger
TagKey-value label on the registered model or on one versionvalidation=passed

Registering needs the CREATE MODEL privilege on the target schema, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on its parents. Loading or serving a model needs EXECUTE on it.

Registering a model

Registration copies a logged model from a run into the registry under a three-level name. If the name does not exist, it is created; each later registration adds a new version. Set the registry to Unity Catalog first, then register from the run URI.

import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient

mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")
mv = mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri=f"runs:/{run_id}/random_forest_model",
    name="ml_prod.churn.churn_classifier",
)
print(mv.name, mv.version)

client = MlflowClient()

A logged model can also be registered at logging time with the registered_model_name argument of the flavor's log_model function. Registration can complete asynchronously, so a new version may briefly be pending before it is ready for use.

Setting and removing tags

Tags are key-value strings. Registered model tags describe the model as a whole, such as an owner or a use case. Version tags describe one version, such as whether it passed validation.

name = "ml_prod.churn.churn_classifier"

client.set_registered_model_tag(name, "owner", "growth-team")
client.set_model_version_tag(name, version="4", key="validation", value="passed")

client.delete_model_version_tag(name, version="4", key="validation")
client.delete_registered_model_tag(name, "owner")

Aliases and the champion and challenger pattern

An alias is a named pointer to exactly one version of a registered model. A version can carry several aliases, and an alias can be moved at any time. Unity Catalog uses aliases instead of stages such as Staging or Production, which do not exist in Unity Catalog.

client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", 4)
client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "challenger", 5)

champion = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion")
client.delete_registered_model_alias(name, "challenger")

model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(f"models:/{name}@champion")

In the champion and challenger pattern, the champion is the version serving production and the challenger is a newly trained candidate. The usual sequence is:

  1. Train the challenger, log its metrics, and register it as a new version.
  2. Point the challenger alias at the new version and evaluate it on the same held-out data as the champion.
  3. If it is better, point the champion alias at the challenger's version. Consumers that load models:/name@champion pick up the change with no code edit.
  4. To roll back, point champion at the previous version. Nothing was deleted, so the rollback is one call.
challenger = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "challenger")
champion = client.get_model_version_by_alias(name, "champion")

new_f1 = client.get_run(challenger.run_id).data.metrics["f1"]
old_f1 = client.get_run(champion.run_id).data.metrics["f1"]

if new_f1 > old_f1:
    client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", challenger.version)

Promoting code versus promoting models

Promote the modelPromote the code (recommended)
What movesThe trained model version, copied through environmentsThe tested training and inference code; each environment trains its own model
StrengthsDeploys the exact artifact that was validated; no retraining needed; useful when training is costly or cannot be repeatedModels are trained on each environment's own data; the code is tested in staging; reproducible and auditable
DrawbacksInference and monitoring code need a separate promotion process; the environment must be able to load the artifactMore compute per environment; results can differ slightly; needs data access and pipelines in every environment
Choose whenTraining data is restricted to one environment, retraining is impractical, or the exact artifact must be provenProduction must retrain on production data, models refresh regularly, or code review and testing gate every release

A model version can be copied across catalogs when a model must move from a development catalog to a production catalog. Registering from a models:/ URI creates a new version under the destination name.

mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")
mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri="models:/dev_catalog.churn.churn_classifier@challenger",
    name="prod_catalog.churn.churn_classifier",
)

Why Unity Catalog beats the workspace registry

CapabilityWorkspace registryUnity Catalog registry
ScopeOne workspaceEvery workspace attached to the same metastore
NamesTwo-part, unqualified by catalogThree-level catalog.schema.model
Access controlWorkspace permissionsGRANT privileges on catalogs, schemas and models
Promotion markersStages such as Staging and ProductionAliases and tags
GovernanceLimited to the workspaceLineage to training data and centralized audit
Gotcha. Stages are a workspace-registry feature. Calls that transition a version to a stage do not apply to Unity Catalog models. Use aliases such as champion and challenger instead.
Exam tip. If a scenario needs one governed model store shared across environments or workspaces, or needs alias-based promotion, the answer is the Unity Catalog registry. Remember the registry URI setting and the three-level name, because omitting either sends the model to the wrong registry.

21. MLOps Principles and Practice

MLOps is the set of practices, processes and technologies for managing data, code and models so that an ML system stays performant, stable and efficient over time. It combines three disciplines, each covering part of the work.

DisciplineFocusKey practices
DataOpsData processing and governanceOptimized processing, centralized discovery and governance, data quality checks, traceable lineage
DevOpsDelivering ML codeMachine learning is code, CI/CD, Git version control, production-grade scheduled jobs
ModelOpsThe model lifecycleTreating models as objects and as data, orchestration and automation of training and deployment

The ML lifecycle

A project moves from a business problem through success criteria, data collection, preprocessing and feature engineering, model training and evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. Development works with static historical data. Production works with continuously changing data, which is why monitoring and retraining belong to the lifecycle rather than being an afterthought.

Core challenges MLOps addresses

  • Reproducibility and experiment tracking. Results differ between environments, and experiments are hard to document. Use tracked runs, versioned code and controlled environments.
  • Model evaluation and comparison. Metric choices and evaluation designs vary, so the best model is hard to pick fairly. Fix the metric, hold out a test set and log every result.
  • Deployment and standardization. Moving a model to production is complex, and each project does it differently. Use standard templates, automated pipelines and versioned, registered models.

Best practices for an MLOps strategy

  • Use a data-centric approach. ML projects are made of data pipelines, which need storage, governance and orchestration.
  • Keep one project code repository in Git and use it in every environment.
  • Separate development, staging and production, and promote changes through them in order.
  • Deploy code rather than model artifacts by default. Promote a model artifact only when the registry chapter's conditions apply.
  • Automate with CI/CD and scheduled jobs rather than manual notebook runs.
  • Set up monitoring, alerting and retraining triggers from the start.

Reference architecture

Infrastructure is set up once per project or team. It includes a Unity Catalog metastore, one or three workspaces, catalogs for dev, staging and prod, a Git repository, and a project template such as Databricks Asset Bundles or MLOps Stacks. Environments can be separated in two ways:

  • Direct separation: a completed workspace per environment. Environments are simpler and the approach scales well to many projects.
  • Indirect separation: one workspace with enforced separation. Infrastructure is simpler and needs fewer permissions, but each environment is more complex and the approach does not scale well.

Each stage has a clear owner and cadence:

StageWho and how oftenTypical work
DevelopmentData scientist; initial build and each updateEDA, ML pipeline development, validation, changes committed to Git
StagingML engineer; every change and every model refreshA pull request triggers CI. Unit, integration and stress tests run; merge to main only when they pass
ProductionML engineer; when changes pass tests or a model needs refreshingA release branch triggers automatic deployment of code, jobs and compute; monitoring, drift detection, retraining

Automation and CI/CD tools

  • Databricks Asset Bundles (recommended): infrastructure as code for jobs, models and pipelines, defined in YAML, versioned with the code and deployed to several workspaces with the CLI.
  • Databricks CLI, SDKs, REST API and Terraform: scripted or infrastructure-driven deployment. SDKs exist for Python, Java, Go and R.
  • Lakeflow Jobs: DAG-based orchestration of notebooks, Python scripts or wheels, SQL, and Spark Declarative Pipelines. Triggers include manual, cron schedule, API, file arrival, Delta table update and continuous.
  • Third-party CI/CD: GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps and Jenkins are common choices. Airflow can also orchestrate Databricks work.
  • Git folders: a visual Git client in the workspace for clone, checkout, commit, push, pull and branch management, authenticated with a personal access token or equivalent.

Advantages of ML runtimes

Databricks Runtime for ML is a cluster runtime with common machine learning libraries and MLflow pre-installed at tested, compatible versions. Its advantages are less setup time, fewer dependency conflicts because versions are tested together, Databricks Autologging enabled by default, GPU-capable variants for deep learning, and a consistent environment that makes results easier to reproduce across clusters. The exact package list depends on the runtime version.

AutoML

Databricks AutoML automates data preparation, feature engineering, model training and selection, and hyperparameter tuning for common problems such as classification, regression and forecasting. It generates editable notebooks, so a team gets a strong baseline quickly and can then add domain expertise.

Monitoring

Monitoring covers four areas: business requirements (the solution still meets its objectives), model performance (accuracy and efficiency over time), resource utilization (cost and SLA compliance), and traceability (audit trails and data lineage).

Drift typeWhat changesTypical sign
Data driftStatistical properties of the input dataFeature distributions shift, such as a new product line changing customer age profiles
Concept driftThe relationship between features and the targetThe same inputs now lead to different outcomes, such as seasonal buying behaviour
Model quality driftPredictive performanceAccuracy, precision, recall or F1 worsen over time
Bias driftOutcomes across groupsPrediction accuracy diverges between groups, creating unfair treatment

Data drift and concept drift can occur together. Responses include collecting new data, retraining the model, and monitoring continuously. Retraining is triggered by a schedule (the recommended starting point), by data changes or detected data drift, by changes to model code or configuration, or by monitoring alerts. Lakehouse Monitoring can monitor tables, views and ML models, including fairness and bias. It computes metrics such as null counts, averages and quantiles over configurable time granularities and data slices, auto-generates dashboards, sends SQL alerts, and stores its results as Delta tables.

Exam tip. Expect scenario questions that ask for the recommended architecture. The correct answer keeps one code repository, separates environments by workspace or catalog, and deploys code through staging before production. Distractors that copy code by hand or skip staging are wrong.

22. Genie Code Fundamentals

Genie Code is an autonomous AI partner for data teams on Databricks. It works across data engineering, data science, machine learning and dashboards. It is grounded in Unity Catalog metadata, semantics and governance, and it can plan and run multi-step workflows while monitoring and resolving issues along the way. For machine learning, it turns natural language requests into the code, tracked runs, registered models and serving endpoints that a manual workflow would build step by step.

Why a language-driven workflow

A traditional model build involves data preparation, feature engineering, training, tuning, evaluation, registration and deployment, each with its own code and tools. Genie Code offers a more flexible, language-driven alternative. The practitioner describes the goal, Genie Code generates and runs the code iteratively, and the practitioner reviews the results and steers the next step. Automated data preparation, feature engineering, training and model selection, and hyperparameter tuning produce notebooks and artifacts that can be explored and changed.

The five ML needs it covers

Tables are referenced in prompts with an @ mention, such as @flights.

Integrations

Genie Code is designed to work with the rest of the Databricks ML stack:

  • Feature Store: the training dataset can be expanded using existing feature tables.
  • MLflow Model Tracking: metrics and parameters of every trial run are tracked, so trials can be compared.
  • Model Registry: generated models can be registered to Unity Catalog.
  • Model Serving: generated models can be deployed to a serving endpoint for real-time inference.
  • Surrounding services: collaborative multi-language notebooks, runtimes and environments, data versioning and monitoring, and both batch scoring (high throughput) and online serving (low latency).

The end-to-end lifecycle

  1. Find the data with a discovery request, then ask for EDA on the chosen table.
  2. Ask for a model. Genie Code builds it, tunes it, and logs every trial run to MLflow.
  3. Compare the tracked runs and choose the candidate that best matches the business goal.
  4. Register the chosen model in Unity Catalog and deploy it to a Model Serving endpoint.
  5. Verify the endpoint returns predictions, then ask for a monitoring dashboard built from the tables.

Evaluating the best model from a session

Because every trial is tracked, the best model is identified by comparing the logged runs. Sort or filter by the metric that fits the problem, such as F1 for imbalanced classification or RMSE for regression. Check the parameters of the top runs, confirm the chosen run is the one registered, and confirm that the endpoint serves that version. Review the generated code too: check the train and test split, look for leakage from target-derived features, and confirm the metric matches the business objective.

Gotcha. Genie Code proposes and executes ML code, but it does not replace review. Its output can use a metric that does not match the business goal, or a split that leaks information. Compare the tracked metrics yourself before promoting a model.
Exam tip. Map each integration to its role. Feature Store supplies training inputs, MLflow Model Tracking records trial metrics and parameters, the Model Registry stores versioned models in Unity Catalog, and Model Serving hosts real-time endpoints.

23. Customizing Genie Code

Genie Code works from general knowledge by default. Customization adds task-specific context in three forms: MCP connections that give access to data and tools, instructions that set standing guidance, and skills that package reusable workflows. Each has a different scope, so the right choice depends on the kind of context being provided.

MechanismWhat it providesWhen it appliesBest for
MCP connectionsAccess to external tools, data sources and metadataWhen the agent needs that context during a taskContext that exists but is hard for an agent to reach
InstructionsStanding guidance written as markdownAlways onStandards, libraries, style and language
SkillsOn-demand bundle of workflow knowledge: markdown with optional scriptsUsed in Agent mode when a task matchesA single repeatable task

MCP connections

MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects Genie Code to external tools and data sources. Use it when important context already exists but is difficult for an AI agent to access. Typical sources are documentation systems, tools and services exposed through APIs, structured data sources, and custom applications. Sources selectable in Databricks include Unity Catalog functions, Vector Search, Genie Spaces, Unity Catalog connections to external MCP servers, and Databricks Apps that serve as custom MCP servers.

Best practices: connect only the sources a workflow needs, choose the source that answers the question most directly, and record what each connection is for so that teammates know when to rely on it.

Instructions

Instructions are markdown files that give Genie Code always-on context: standards, preferred libraries, style and language. They can be configured at the workspace level, which suits team standards, or at the user level, which suits personal preferences.

Best practices: write clear, specific instructions; keep them under 20,000 characters; use headings and delimiters so the structure is easy to follow; keep the scope broadly relevant to all tasks; and provide context and references where they help.

# Team ML standards
## Language and libraries
- Use Python with scikit-learn, and PySpark for large tables.
## Experiment tracking
- Log every run to /Shared/churn-experiments.
## Registration
- Register final models to ml_prod.churn in Unity Catalog.
- Set the champion alias only after metrics are reviewed.

Skills

Skills are on-demand bundles of domain knowledge and workflow, written as markdown with optional scripts. They are used in Agent mode for task-specific procedures, examples and automation. Because they load only when relevant, they are the right place for detailed procedures that would clutter the always-on instructions.

Best practices: focus each skill on a single task or workflow; give it a clear, descriptive name; provide step-by-step examples; include only the context the task needs; iterate and refine it as the workflow changes; and separate guidance from automation, keeping the explanation in markdown and the executable steps in scripts.

# Register and promote a classifier
## When to use
Use after a training run has logged its metrics.
## Steps
1. Find the run with the highest F1 in the shared experiment.
2. Register it to ml_prod.churn.churn_classifier.
3. Point the challenger alias at the new version and report its metrics.

Choosing the right mechanism

  • A standard that should always apply, such as a naming rule or a preferred library, belongs in instructions.
  • A repeatable procedure that applies only to certain tasks, such as registering and promoting a model, belongs in a skill.
  • Knowledge that lives in an external system, such as documentation or a governed table, belongs behind an MCP connection.

Choosing the wrong mechanism causes problems. A rule buried in a skill is missed when the task does not match. A long procedure in instructions consumes context on every task.

End-to-end use

  1. Write the team's standards as workspace-level instructions.
  2. Connect the MCP sources the team relies on, such as a Genie Space holding the data dictionary.
  3. Add a skill for each repeatable workflow, such as training and registering a classifier.
  4. Prompt Genie Code through the workflow in natural language: EDA, training, tuning, and logging trial runs.
  5. Review the tracked runs, register the chosen model to Unity Catalog, and move the champion alias after review.
  6. Deploy the model to a serving endpoint and verify that it returns predictions.
Gotcha. Instructions have a 20,000-character limit. Content that grows past it should move into skills, which load only when a matching task runs.
Exam tip. Pick the mechanism by its scope. Always-on standards are instructions. A workflow triggered by a task is a skill. Access to external context or tools is an MCP connection. Scenario answers that use a skill for a rule that must always apply are wrong.
